UNIT 2 · TRAVEL AND TOURISMB1 PRE-INTERMEDIATE

Travel and tourism

Lessons 2A + 2C · We had an adventure past simple · tourism · asking for information in a public place

In this booklet

1 Reading — the last page rule 1

2 Grammar — past simple 3

3 Vocabulary — tourism 6

4 Listening — day three: water skiing 8

5 Everyday English — asking for information 10

You will learn to

— talk about a past holiday using the past simple

— use was / were and did in the right places — they are two systems

— say -ed endings correctly, and know which ones add a syllable

— use a lexical set about tourism

— ask for information in a station or a tourist office, and come back for one more thing

Prepared by Olimov Azamat

1

Reading · the last page rule

1.1 Discuss. When you go somewhere new, do you plan everything or decide on the day? Which is better?

KEY WORDS

a guidebook a book about a place for tourists

a landmark a famous building or place

a souvenir something you buy to remember a trip

a rule something you decide always to do

The Last Page Rule

Every guidebook has the same shape. The famous things come first, with photographs, and at the end of each chapter there is a short section called something like Also worth a look. Nobody reads it. Last April I decided to read nothing else.

DAY ONE. I arrived in the afternoon and I did not go to the cathedral. Instead I went to a museum of clocks, which the book gave four lines and no photograph. There were eleven visitors, including me and a school group of eight. The man who sold me the ticket was also the man who explained the clocks, and when I asked a question he stopped the tour and talked to me for twenty minutes. I have never had that in a famous museum.

DAY TWO. The book mentioned a market on the north side of the river, but only to say that it mainly serves local residents. That turned out to mean there were no souvenirs, which was the best thing about it. I ate breakfast standing up next to two taxi drivers, I bought a kilo of apricots I could not carry, and nobody tried to sell me anything at all.

DAY THREE. This is where the rule stopped being charming. The last page of the walks chapter suggested a path along an old railway line. It did not say how long it was. I started at nine, I ran out of water at one, and I arrived back at half past five with sunburn and one working phone battery between me and the hotel. I did not enjoy any of it, and I am glad I did it.

Would I recommend the rule? Not for a short trip, and not in August. But I saw a city that eleven other people saw that week, and I still remember all three days — which is more than I can say for the holiday I took last year, where I did everything correctly.

2

Grammar · past simple

PRESENTATION

The past simple is for a finished action at a finished time — yesterday, last April, in 2019, three hours ago.

+ Positive — regular verbs add -ed. arrive → arrived · start → started · stop → stopped · carry → carried. Irregular verbs change. go → went · buy → bought · see → saw · eat → ate · have → had

− Negative — didn't + the bare infinitive. I didn't go to the cathedral. Never didn't went. The -ed and the vowel change live in did, so the main verb goes back to its plain form.

? Questions — did + subject + bare infinitive. Did you have a good week? · What did you buy?

be be is different — no did at all. Some of my experiences weren't very good. · What was your favourite thing? · Were you tired?

So there are two systems, not one. be → was / were / wasn't / weren't / Was…? / Were…? · everything else → did / didn't.

with be

with every other verb

positive

It was hot.

I went to the market.

negative

They weren't very good.

I didn't like the mosquitoes.

question

Was it your first time?

Did you have a good week?

wh- question

What was your favourite thing?

Where did you stay?

ERROR WARNING

Four mistakes. The first two are the ones your teacher will hear in every lesson this term:

1 Double past. I didn't went. ✗ → I didn't go. ✓ · Did you saw it? ✗ → Did you see it? ✓ Once did is there, the main verb is finished with the past.

2 did with be. Did it was hot? ✗ → Was it hot? ✓ · It didn't was expensive. ✗ → It wasn't expensive. ✓

3 Word order in questions. Where you went? ✗ → Where did you go? ✓ The auxiliary comes before the subject, every time.

4 Spelling. stoped ✗ → stopped ✓ · carryed ✗ → carried ✓ · arrivedd ✗ → arrived ✓ One vowel + one consonant doubles; a final -y after a consonant becomes -ied; a verb already ending in -e just adds -d.

Vocabulary · tourism

PRESENTATION

Where you stay: a hotel · a hostel · a guest house · a campsite · self-catering (you cook yourself) · all-inclusive (everything is in the price)

What you do: go sightseeing · go on a day trip · take a guided tour · visit a landmark · check in and check out · unpack

What you take and buy: a suitcase · hand luggage · suntan lotion · a guidebook · a souvenir · a postcard

The people and places: a travel agent · a receptionist · a tour guide · a tourist office · the coast · the seaside

Careful with two of them. A travel agent is a person; the shop is a travel agent's. And make a photo is not English — you take a photo.

PRONUNCIATION — THE -ED ENDING

Three sounds, one rule, and only one of them adds a syllable.

/ɪd/ — an extra syllable. Only after /t/ or /d/: wanted · needed · started · decided · waited · included · shouted · ended

/t/ — no extra syllable. After a voiceless sound: asked · looked · watched · stopped

/d/ — no extra syllable. After a voiced sound: changed · played · arrived · smiled · believed

Why it matters. Wanted is two syllables and watched is one. Students who add a syllable to everything sound as if they are reading; students who add it to nothing lose the past tense entirely.

Listening · day three: water skiing

BEFORE YOU LISTEN

Richard spent a week saying yes to every question. On day one a travel agent sold him a beach holiday he did not want; on day two he bought three hats he did not need. Now it is day three, and yesterday he agreed to a water skiing lesson.

If your class has the audio, this is the day-three recording. If not, your teacher will read the script — the tasks are the same.

4.1 Before listening. Do you think he enjoyed it? Tell a partner why or why not.

4.2 Listen once. True (T) or false (F)? Correct the false ones.

1 The class began with a lesson on the beach before they went out to sea.

2 Richard felt fine when they went out on the boat.

3 He found it difficult to stand up on the water skis.

4 He hated water skiing.

5 When he got back to the hotel, he went straight to bed.

4.3 Listen again and complete each line.

1 I badly the night before, so I was tired.

2 The instructor us how to hold the rope.

3 I up on the third try — and immediately fell over.

4 I I was going to hate it.

5 The receptionist me another question, and you know what I said.

WHY YOU DIDN'T HEAR IT

The -ed you can't hear. In asked me the /t/ disappears almost completely between the /k/ and the /m/: /ɑːsmi/. In stopped talking the /t/ of stopped joins the /t/ of talking and you hear one sound.

So the past tense often survives only in the irregular verbs and in did. Listen for those, and assume the regular verbs around them are past too.

5

Everyday English · asking for information

LISTENING INTO SPEAKING

Annie is at a railway station. She needs a ticket to Birmingham — and then, on her way out, she realises she has forgotten something.

5.1 Listen to Part 1 and answer.

1 When does the next train to Birmingham leave, and how often do the trains go?

2 Which platform does it leave from?

3 How much is the ticket, and how does she pay?

4 What does she want to get from the newsagent's?

ASKING FOR INFORMATION IN A PUBLIC PLACE

Six questions that will get you through a station, an airport or a tourist office anywhere:

What time's the next train? · How often do the trains leave? · How much is a ticket?

Could you tell me where the ticket office is? · Can I pay by card? · Where can I buy a magazine?

The polite one is worth learning whole. After Could you tell me where… the word order goes back to normal: Could you tell me where the ticket office is? — not where is the ticket office. The question is already asked by Could you.

What the assistant says: Yes, how can I help you? · Is there anything else I can help you with?

AT THE TOURIST OFFICE

A Hi, (1) where the museum is, please? B Yes, it's not far — it's by the river. Look on the map, here.

A I see. And (2) does it open? B From 8 am till 4 pm.

A (3) is a ticket? B For adults, it's £14.

A (4) buy a ticket? B I can sell you one here, or you can buy one at the museum.

A Oh, I'll buy one here. (5) pay by card? B Of course — that's no problem.

ASKING FOR MORE INFORMATION

You have finished, you have turned away, and then you remember something. Two phrases do this job, and both of them are apologies before they are questions:

Sorry, just one more thing. — you are interrupting again, and you know it.

Actually, there is one more thing. — used when the assistant has just asked Is there anything else? and you said no.

Without them, a second question sounds like a demand. With them, it sounds like a person.

5.4 Which phrase would you use? Write A (Sorry, just one more thing) or B (Actually, there is one more thing).

1 You have already said goodbye and walked away.

3 You are still at the desk and remember a question.

2 The assistant said anything else? and you said no.

4 You are coming back after two minutes.

PRONUNCIATION — CONNECTED SPEECH

There is no pause when a consonant sound comes before a vowel sound. The two words join, and English speakers hear one word where you see two.

Where can I buy a magazine? → /kənaɪ/ · How much is a ticket? → /ɪzə/

This is why Can I sounds like cannai and why students who pause between every word are harder to follow, not easier.
